questions.prompt: Which of the following is an inner product on the vector space of all real-valued continuous functions on $[0,1]$?
hints: Test bilinearity and positive definiteness separately.
For the integral without absolute values, continuity makes a nonzero square positive on an interval.
questions.solution: Option D is symmetric and bilinear. Its diagonal value is $\int_0^1 f^2\ge0$. If $f(t_0)\ne0$, continuity gives an interval of positive length on which $f^2$ is bounded below by a positive constant, so the integral is strictly positive. Hence it is an inner product. A and B fail homogeneity for negative scalars: with $f=g=1$, replacing $f$ by $-f$ leaves their value at 1 instead of changing it to $-1$. C is bilinear but not positive definite: $f(t)=t(1-t)$ is nonzero while its two endpoint values vanish.
questions.theory: A real inner product is a symmetric bilinear form that is positive definite: $\langle f,f\rangle>0$ for every nonzero vector. Positivity alone is not sufficient; absolute values applied to a bilinear expression normally destroy linearity under negative scalars. On a space of continuous functions, integration against a strictly positive continuous weight gives an inner product because a nonzero continuous function remains nonzero on a set of positive length. Endpoint evaluation instead gives a positive semidefinite form with a large nullspace. The induced norm is the square root of the diagonal form, and Cauchy–Schwarz then bounds the mixed integral. The integral norm does not equal the uniform norm, and this continuous-function space need not be complete in that norm. Always identify the underlying vector space before deciding whether a diagonal form has a nontrivial kernel.

similar_questions.prompt: Is $\int_0^1 t f(t)g(t)\,dt$ an inner product on $C[0,1]$?
similar_questions.solution: It is symmetric and bilinear. A nonzero continuous $f$ is nonzero on an interval containing some positive $t$, where $tf^2>0$. Its integral is positive, so yes.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the nullspace of $f(0)g(0)+f(1/2)g(1/2)$.
similar_questions.solution: The diagonal value is $f(0)^2+f(1/2)^2$. It vanishes exactly when both evaluations vanish. Thus the nullspace consists of all continuous functions with $f(0)=f(1/2)=0$, including $f(t)=t(t-1/2)$.

questions.prompt: Define $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ to be positive when $\langle Av,v\rangle\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$. Let $A_{\alpha,\beta}=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&1&1\\1&0&0\\1&0&\beta\end{pmatrix}$ and $S=\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb R^2:A_{\alpha,\beta}\text{ is positive}\}$. Which statement is true?
hints: Inspect the principal submatrix on the first two coordinates.
Test $v=(1,t,0)^T$ and vary $t$.
questions.solution: For $v=(1,t,0)^T$, $v^TA_{\alpha,\beta}v=\alpha+2t$. For every fixed $\alpha$, choosing $t<-\alpha/2$ makes this negative, independently of $\beta$. Thus no parameter pair belongs to $S$, and A is true. B and C each admit many pairs but none can actually be positive; D fails for the same reason. Equivalently, the principal $2\times2$ determinant is $\det\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=-1$, incompatible with positive semidefiniteness.
questions.theory: A real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite when its quadratic form is nonnegative on every real vector. This differs from positive definite, which requires strict positivity for every nonzero vector. Restricting the quadratic form to coordinate subspaces shows that every principal submatrix must also be positive semidefinite, and consequently every principal minor must be nonnegative. In particular, a zero diagonal entry forces every off-diagonal entry in the same row and column to vanish: otherwise a quadratic expression with a free linear term becomes negative for one choice of the second coordinate. For a symmetric matrix, eigenvalues are real and positive semidefiniteness is equivalent to all eigenvalues being nonnegative. Directly constructing a negative test vector is often faster than calculating eigenvalues or all minors. Conditions involving the full determinant alone are generally insufficient.

similar_questions.prompt: For which $a,b$ is $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&0\end{pmatrix}$ positive semidefinite?
similar_questions.solution: Its quadratic form is $ax^2+2bxy$. Taking $x=1$ and varying $y$ forces $b=0$; then nonnegativity forces $a\ge0$. These conditions also suffice.

similar_questions.prompt: Is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ positive definite?
similar_questions.solution: Its quadratic form is $2x^2+2xy+2y^2=(x+y)^2+x^2+y^2>0$ for every nonzero pair. Therefore it is positive definite; its eigenvalues are 1 and 3.

questions.prompt: A function $f:\mathbb C\mapsto\mathbb C$ is said to be analytic at $\infty$ if $g(w)=f(1/w)$ is analytic at 0 after an appropriate value is assigned to $g(0)$. Which statement is true?

options.A: Any nonconstant polynomial is analytic at $\infty$
options.B: If $f$ is analytic at $\infty$ then $f$ is bounded
options.C: For any $z_0\in\mathbb C$, the function $f(z)=e^{1/z-z_0}$ is analytic at $\infty$
options.D: Any entire function can be extended to an analytic function at $\infty$

hints: Use the coordinate $w=1/z$ to move infinity to zero.
For option C, substitution produces an exponential analytic at $w=0$.
questions.solution: Under the printed exponent $1/z-z_0$, option C gives $g(w)=e^{w-z_0}$, which is entire and has $g(0)=e^{-z_0}$. Thus its germ near infinity is analytic. A is false: a degree-$m>0$ polynomial becomes a function with a pole of order $m$ at zero. D is false, for example for $f(z)=z$. B would be true for an entire $f$ by Liouville, but the premise states only analyticity near infinity. A function can equal zero for $|z|>2$ and take unbounded values inside that disk, so analyticity at infinity alone does not imply global boundedness. C has a finite singularity at zero; the assertion concerns its behavior near infinity, and any assigned value at zero leaves that behavior unchanged.
questions.theory: The point at infinity on the Riemann sphere has local coordinate $w=1/z$. A function is analytic at infinity precisely when its expression in this coordinate extends holomorphically through $w=0$. Equivalently, it is holomorphic outside a sufficiently large disk and has a removable singularity in the inverted coordinate. Such a function is bounded near infinity, but global boundedness requires additional control on the finite plane. If it is also entire, compactness of each closed finite disk supplies that control, and Liouville implies that the function is constant. Nonconstant polynomials instead have poles at infinity; nonpolynomial entire functions have essential singularities there. A finite singularity does not prevent analyticity at infinity. When an elementary formula excludes a finite point, distinguish that domain issue from the local assertion at infinity.

similar_questions.prompt: Classify infinity for $f(z)=z^3+2z$.
similar_questions.solution: Substitution gives $g(w)=w^{-3}+2w^{-1}$, so zero is a pole of order 3. Infinity is therefore a pole of order 3, not an analytic point.

similar_questions.prompt: Is $f(z)=1/(z-2)$ analytic at infinity?
similar_questions.solution: Its inverted expression is $g(w)=w/(1-2w)$, holomorphic for $|w|<1/2$ and equal to zero at zero. Thus infinity is removable even though $f$ has a pole at the finite point 2.

questions.prompt: Define $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ by $f(z)=\bigl||z|^2-1\bigr|^2$. Which statement is true?

options.A: $f$ is complex differentiable at all complex numbers except $z\in\{0,1\}$

hints: Write $f=u+iv$ in Cartesian coordinates; here $v=0$.
Both partial derivatives of $u=(x^2+y^2-1)^2$ must vanish.
questions.solution: The literal formula is $u(x,y)=(x^2+y^2-1)^2$, $v=0$. The Cauchy–Riemann conditions are $4x(x^2+y^2-1)=0$ and $4y(x^2+y^2-1)=0$. Since these partial derivatives are continuous, the conditions are necessary and sufficient at each point. They hold exactly at $z=0$ or $|z|=1$, and the derivative is zero there. Hence A, B, C and D are all false as printed: for example $z=i$ is differentiable but is absent from B–D, while $z=2$ is not differentiable and refutes A. If D were intended to read “$z=0$ or $|z|=1$”, that corrected option would be true. That correction is not made in the transcription or answer labels.
questions.theory: For a complex function $f=u+iv$ with continuous first partial derivatives near a point, complex differentiability at that point is equivalent to the Cauchy–Riemann equations $u_x=v_y$ and $u_y=-v_x$. A real-valued function has $v=0$, so these equations require both real partial derivatives of $u$ to vanish. Complex differentiability at isolated points or along a curve is possible without holomorphy on an open set. A nonconstant real-valued holomorphic function cannot exist on a connected open set, as follows from the Cauchy–Riemann equations or the open mapping theorem. Squared absolute values of real expressions simplify before differentiation. The most important diagnostic here is to solve the entire locus of the gradient equations; testing just the real points 0 and 1 misses other points on the unit circle.

similar_questions.prompt: Where is $f(z)=|z|^2$ complex differentiable?
similar_questions.solution: Here $u=x^2+y^2$, so $u_x=2x$ and $u_y=2y$. Both vanish only at zero; continuous partials ensure differentiability there, with derivative zero.

similar_questions.prompt: Where is $f(z)=(|z|^2-4)^2$ complex differentiable?

questions.prompt: Let $f,g$ be entire functions with $\lim_{z\to\infty}f(z)/z^n=\lim_{z\to\infty}g(z)/z^n=1$, for a fixed positive integer $n$. Which statement is true?

options.B: $f-g$ is necessarily a polynomial of degree at most $n-1$
options.C: There exist such $f,g$ for which $f-g$ is a polynomial of degree $n$
options.D: There exist such $f,g$ for which $f-g$ is not a polynomial

hints: The limits give polynomial growth bounds on both entire functions.
Cauchy coefficient estimates eliminate degrees above $n$, and the leading coefficients agree.
questions.solution: For sufficiently large $|z|$, $|f(z)|,|g(z)|\le2|z|^n$. Cauchy estimates on circles of radius $R$ imply that Taylor coefficients above degree $n$ vanish as $R\to\infty$. Thus $f,g$ are polynomials of degree at most $n$, and each limit forces its degree to be exactly $n$ with leading coefficient 1. Their leading terms cancel, so $f-g$ has degree at most $n-1$ (or is zero), proving B. A fails with $f=z^n$, $g=z^n+1$; C fails by leading-term cancellation; D fails because both functions are polynomials.
questions.theory: An entire function with polynomial growth is a polynomial. More precisely, if $|h(z)|\le C(1+|z|^m)$ globally for some integer $m\ge0$, Cauchy estimates give $|h^{(k)}(0)|/k!\le C(1+R^m)/R^k$ for every circle of radius $R$. Letting $R$ tend to infinity makes all coefficients with $k>m$ zero. A bound outside a disk can be extended to a global bound using the maximum of the continuous function on that disk. A complex limit at infinity is uniform over all directions outside sufficiently large disks, a stronger hypothesis than a limit on the positive real axis. After polynomiality is established, division by $z^n$ identifies the degree and leading coefficient. Equal leading coefficients yield cancellation, but do not imply equality of all lower-order terms.

similar_questions.prompt: If an entire $h$ satisfies $h(z)/z^2\to3$, describe $h$.
similar_questions.solution: The limit bounds $h$ by a multiple of $|z|^2$ outside a disk. Cauchy estimates force degree at most 2, and the limit identifies the coefficient of $z^2$ as 3. Thus $h(z)=3z^2+az+b$.

similar_questions.prompt: If entire $h$ is $o(|z|)$ at infinity, what is $h$?
similar_questions.solution: Cauchy estimates for $k\ge1$ give $|h^{(k)}(0)|/k!\le M(R)/R^k$ with $M(R)=o(R)$. Every positive-order coefficient vanishes, including $k=1$, so $h$ is constant.

questions.prompt: Let $f$ be holomorphic on $\{|z|<2\}$. Its only zero in $\{|z|\le1\}$ is a simple zero at the origin. For the positively oriented unit circle $\gamma$, find $\int_\gamma dz/f(z)$.

questions.solution: Simplicity gives $f(z)=zh(z)$ near zero, with $h$ holomorphic and $h(0)=f\prime(0)\ne0$. Therefore $\operatorname{Res}_{0}(1/f)=\lim_{z\to0}z/f(z)=1/f\prime(0)$. There are no other poles inside or on the circle, so the residue theorem gives $2\pi i/f\prime(0)$, option C. A reverses the reciprocal and is not generally equal. B and D use the second derivative, which does not determine this residue and may even vanish, as in $f(z)=z$. Positive orientation determines the plus sign.
questions.theory: The residue theorem states that the integral of a meromorphic function around a positively oriented simple closed contour is $2\pi i$ times the sum of residues of its interior poles, provided no singularity lies on the contour. If a holomorphic function has a simple zero at $a$, then its derivative at $a$ is nonzero and its reciprocal has a simple pole with residue $1/f\prime(a)$. This follows directly from the first-order Taylor expansion, or from the factorization $f(z)=(z-a)h(z)$ with $h(a)=f\prime(a)$. At a multiple zero, higher coefficients matter and the simple reciprocal formula is no longer applicable. Always check both the multiplicity of zeros and the absence of boundary zeros. Reversing the orientation changes the sign of the integral.

similar_questions.prompt: Compute $\oint_{|z|=2}dz/[z(z-1)]$.
similar_questions.solution: There are simple poles at 0 and 1. Their residues are $-1$ and 1, whose sum is zero. Hence the integral is zero, illustrating that each interior zero must be counted.

hints: Work modulo 100.

Thus $3^{2019}\equiv3^{19}\equiv3^{-1}\pmod{100}$. The inverse is 67 because $3\cdot67=201\equiv1\pmod{100}$. questions.theory: Last digits are residues modulo a power of ten: the last two digits are determined modulo 100. When a base is coprime to the modulus, its powers form a periodic sequence in the multiplicative group of units. Euler gives an exponent dividing $\varphi(m)$, while direct computation can reveal a shorter period. Exponents should only be reduced modulo a verified period; reducing modulo 100 itself is not valid. A negative exponent denotes a multiplicative inverse and is legitimate only for a unit. The Chinese remainder theorem also allows computation modulo 4 and 25 and reconstruction modulo 100. For bases sharing factors with 100, Euler does not apply, and prime-power valuations must be examined separately. Leading zeroes should be retained when a last-two-digit residue is below ten.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the last two digits of $3^{40}$.
similar_questions.solution: Since $3^{20}\equiv1\pmod{100}$, squaring gives $3^{40}\equiv1$. The last two digits are 01.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the last two digits of $7^{2020}$.
similar_questions.solution: $7^2=49$ and $7^4=2401\equiv1\pmod{100}$. As 2020 is divisible by 4, the residue is 1 and the last two digits are 01.

questions.prompt: Let $G$ be a group of order 2020. Which statement is necessarily true?
hints: Factor 2020 and apply Sylow to the largest prime.
The number of Sylow 101-subgroups divides 20 and is congruent to 1 modulo 101.
questions.solution: $2020=2^2\cdot5\cdot101$. The number $n_{101}$ of Sylow 101-subgroups divides 20 and satisfies $n_{101}\equiv1\pmod{101}$, forcing $n_{101}=1$. Its unique Sylow subgroup has order 101 and is normal, nontrivial and proper. Thus G is not simple, proving A. B is false for cyclic $C_{2020}$, which has one subgroup per divisor and therefore 11 proper subgroups. C and D are not forced: $D_{10}\times C_{202}$ has order 2020 and is nonabelian, hence noncyclic, where $D_{10}$ denotes the dihedral group of order 10.
questions.theory: Sylow theorems describe subgroups whose orders are the maximal powers of a prime dividing a finite group order. If $p^a$ is that maximal power, Sylow $p$-subgroups exist, are conjugate, and their number divides the cofactor and is congruent to 1 modulo $p$. A unique Sylow subgroup is normal because conjugation cannot send it to a different subgroup. A simple group has no nontrivial proper normal subgroup, so proving uniqueness immediately disproves simplicity when the Sylow subgroup is proper. These numerical restrictions do not generally establish commutativity or cyclicity. To reject a universal claim about groups of a given order, construct a group of that order violating it; direct products often provide convenient counterexamples. Cyclic groups have exactly one subgroup for each positive divisor of their order.

similar_questions.prompt: Can a group of order 55 be simple?
similar_questions.solution: $55=5\cdot11$. Its Sylow 11-subgroup count divides 5 and is 1 modulo 11, so it is 1. The normal subgroup of order 11 is proper and nontrivial; the group is not simple.

similar_questions.prompt: How many proper subgroups does a cyclic group of order 12 have?
similar_questions.solution: The divisors are 1,2,3,4,6,12, with one subgroup of each order. Excluding the whole group of order 12 leaves five proper subgroups, including the trivial subgroup.

questions.prompt: Which statement is NOT true?

options.A: The polynomial ring $\mathbb Z[x]$ is a Principal Ideal Domain (PID)
options.B: The polynomial ring $\mathbb Q[x]$ is a Principal Ideal Domain (PID)
options.C: The polynomial ring $\mathbb Z[x]$ is a Unique Factorization Domain (UFD)
options.D: The polynomial ring $\mathbb Q[x]$ is a Unique Factorization Domain (UFD)

hints: Over a field, polynomial division gives a Euclidean domain.
In $\mathbb Z[x]$, inspect the ideal $(2,x)$.
questions.solution: $\mathbb Q[x]$ is Euclidean by polynomial degree, hence a PID and a UFD, so B and D are true. Gauss lemma implies $\mathbb Z[x]$ is a UFD because $\mathbb Z$ is a UFD, giving C. However $(2,x)$ is not principal. A hypothetical generator divides both 2 and x, and thus must be a unit: a constant divisor of x in $\mathbb Z[x]$ is $\pm1$. But $(2,x)$ is proper, since evaluation at zero followed by reduction modulo 2 maps the quotient onto $\mathbb F_2$ and annihilates this ideal. Hence A is the false statement.
questions.theory: A principal ideal domain is an integral domain in which every ideal has a single generator. A unique factorization domain requires every nonzero nonunit to factor into irreducibles uniquely up to order and multiplication by units. Every Euclidean domain is a PID, and every PID is a UFD; the converses need not hold. Polynomial rings over fields are Euclidean using degree because division by a nonzero leading coefficient is possible. Gauss lemma extends unique factorization from a UFD to its polynomial ring, but does not extend the PID property. A useful obstruction is an ideal generated by a nonunit integer and an indeterminate. To show it is not principal, combine divisibility of any hypothetical generator with properness of the ideal, often witnessed by a homomorphism to a finite field.

similar_questions.prompt: Why is $(3,x)$ not principal in $\mathbb Z[x]$?
similar_questions.solution: A generator would divide both 3 and x. It must be a constant unit, so its ideal would be the whole ring. Yet evaluation at zero modulo 3 annihilates $(3,x)$ and sends 1 to 1, proving properness and contradiction.

similar_questions.prompt: Is $\mathbb R[x]$ a PID?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. For a nonzero ideal choose a polynomial of least degree. Divide every other polynomial in the ideal by it; the remainder has smaller degree and lies in the ideal, so it vanishes. This polynomial generates the ideal.

questions.prompt: Suppose $f:[0,1]\times[0,1]\to(0,1)\times(0,1)$ is continuous and nonconstant. Which statement is NOT true in general?

options.D: The image of $f$ has nonempty interior

Can the square map continuously onto a line segment lying inside the target square?
questions.solution: The domain is compact and path connected. Its continuous image is therefore compact and path connected, proving B and C. Since $f$ is nonconstant, its image contains distinct points $a,b$. The continuous distance map $p\mapsto\|p-a\|$ on the connected image contains the entire interval $[0,\|b-a\|]$, so the image is uncountable, proving A. D fails for $f(x,y)=(1/4+x/2,1/2)$, whose image is a nondegenerate horizontal segment with empty interior in the plane. Thus D is the assertion not guaranteed.
questions.theory: Compactness is preserved under a continuous map: an open cover of the image pulls back to an open cover of the compact domain and hence has a finite subcover. Connectedness and path connectedness are likewise preserved, with a path transported by composition. A connected subset of Euclidean space containing two different points must be uncountable, as a continuous real-valued distance function has an interval in its range. Having nonempty interior is a separate dimensional property and is not preserved by continuous maps, even when the domain has nonempty interior. The image may collapse to a curve or segment. Nonconstancy rules out a singleton but does not prevent this collapse. Specify the ambient space when discussing interior: a segment has empty planar interior but nonempty relative interior in its supporting line.

similar_questions.prompt: Give a continuous nonconstant map from a disk with image of empty planar interior.
similar_questions.solution: On the unit disk take $f(x,y)=(x,0)$. Its image is the segment $[-1,1]\times\{0\}$, which is compact and path connected but has empty interior in $\mathbb R^2$.

similar_questions.prompt: Can a connected set have exactly two points?
similar_questions.solution: No in a Hausdorff metric space. If the points are $a\ne b$, disjoint sufficiently small balls separate them into two nonempty relatively open subsets. Thus the two-point set is disconnected.

questions.prompt: Consider $t\dot y-3y=t^2y^{1/2}$, $y(1)=1$. Find $y(2)$.
hints: On the positive solution branch set $u=\sqrt y$.
The resulting linear equation is $u\prime-3u/(2t)=t/2$.
questions.solution: Let $y=u^2$ with $u>0$ near 1. Then $2tu u\prime-3u^2=t^2u$, so $u\prime-\frac{3}{2t}u=\frac t2$. Multiplying by $t^{-3/2}$ gives $(t^{-3/2}u)\prime=\frac12t^{-1/2}$. Hence $u=t^2+Ct^{3/2}$. The condition $u(1)=1$ gives $C=0$, so $y=t^4$ and $y(2)=16$, B. This branch stays positive for $t\in[1,2]$, making all divisions valid; direct substitution yields $t\dot y-3y=t^4=t^2\sqrt y$. The other numerical values do not satisfy the derived value.
questions.theory: Bernoulli equations have the form $y\prime+P(t)y=Q(t)y^r$ with $r\ne0,1$. On a branch where the required powers are defined and the solution is nonzero, the substitution $u=y^{1-r}$ turns them into linear first-order equations. An integrating factor $\exp(\int P)$ then permits direct integration. For a square-root equation, the real-valued unknown must be nonnegative, and $u=\sqrt y$ denotes the nonnegative branch; arbitrary negative solutions of the transformed linear equation cannot simply be squared and accepted. Dividing by the root also excludes zeros, so check whether the resulting branch reaches zero. Local uniqueness is standard where the right-hand side is continuously differentiable in y away from zero. Direct substitution and the initial value provide essential checks on the calculation.

similar_questions.prompt: Solve $y\prime=2\sqrt y$, $y(0)=1$, while $y>0$.
similar_questions.solution: Put $u=\sqrt y$. Then $2uu\prime=2u$, hence $u\prime=1$ and $u=t+1$. Thus $y=(t+1)^2$ for $t>-1$; on that interval the positive-root branch agrees with $u$.

similar_questions.prompt: Solve $y\prime+y=\sqrt y$, $y(0)=1$, on its positive branch.

questions.solution: Literal substitution gives $(A-2I)\vec a=0$, with $A-2I=\begin{pmatrix}-1&2&2\\2&-2&1\\0&2&\lambda-3\end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant is $[-1][-2(\lambda-3)-2]-2[2(\lambda-3)]+2[4]=16-2\lambda$. If $\vec a\ne0$ is intended, this forces $\lambda=8$, absent from all four options. At $\lambda=8$, a valid eigenvector is $(6,5,-2)^T$, as direct substitution confirms. In addition, the printed statement does not require $\vec a\ne0$: the zero vector solves the system for every $\lambda$, so its literal hypothesis imposes no restriction at all. With the conventional nonzero interpretation, the derived answer remains 8, not any listed choice. No alternative third equation is invented.
questions.theory: A constant-coefficient linear system $x\prime=Ax$ has an exponential solution $x(t)=ae^{rt}$ exactly when $Aa=ra$. For a nonzero vector a, this means r is an eigenvalue and the characteristic determinant $\det(A-rI)$ vanishes. The zero vector is always a solution and never imposes an eigenvalue condition, so a nontriviality premise is essential when inferring parameters. Once a parameter is obtained, an eigenvector and direct substitution check both the determinant arithmetic and the transcription. Several terms in one equation may involve the same coordinate and must be combined as printed before forming the matrix. When no listed option satisfies the necessary determinant condition, report the discrepancy explicitly instead of altering a coefficient to manufacture an available answer. Eigenvectors are defined only for nonzero vectors.

similar_questions.prompt: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&\lambda\end{pmatrix}$, when does a nonzero $ae^{3t}$ solve $x\prime=Ax$?
similar_questions.solution: $\det(A-3I)=(-2)(\lambda-3)$ must vanish, so $\lambda=3$. Then $-2a_1+a_2=0$ and $(1,2)^T$ is an eigenvector, giving the required solution.

A formal invariant formula may satisfy the equation away from a characteristic but lose differentiability on it. Real cube roots are continuous at zero but have unbounded derivatives there, so continuity alone does not establish a classical solution.

This condition is not automatically sufficient: substitute a polynomial of the resulting degree to determine lower coefficients and check existence. Exceptional small degrees, especially constants, deserve separate attention because their derivatives vanish. The zero polynomial solves every homogeneous linear equation but has no ordinary degree and is not a candidate in a degree question. Balancing leading terms is typically faster than finding all nonpolynomial solutions of the equation.

questions.prompt: Newton–Raphson approximates $\sqrt\alpha$ for $\alpha>0$. For the error $e_n=x_n-\sqrt\alpha$, which recurrence holds?

Since $x_n=e_n+s$, $e_{n+1}=e_n^2/[2(e_n+s)]$, exactly C. A and B incorrectly apply the iteration to the error itself. D has a different denominator; it does not coincide with the derived identity except in special accidental cases. Near the positive root, the coefficient tends to $1/(2s)$, demonstrating quadratic convergence.
questions.theory: Newton–Raphson for a scalar equation $f(x)=0$ uses $x_{n+1}=x_n-f(x_n)/f\prime(x_n)$ when the derivative is nonzero. For a simple root with sufficient smoothness and a sufficiently close initial value, the method converges quadratically: the next error is bounded by a constant times the square of the current error. An exact error identity is especially useful for the square-root iteration, because it also reveals the allowed denominator and the sign of subsequent errors. Positive starting values remain positive, and after one step the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality places the iterate at or above the positive root. Distinguish the iterate from its error when substituting. The recurrence is undefined if an iterate is zero; convergence guarantees and algebraic identities should always state the domain where the iteration itself is defined.

The other curve types do not describe this equation. Equivalently, integrating $x^2y\prime$ by parts leaves the endpoint term plus $\int_0^5(y^2-2xy)dx$, whose fixed-endpoint stationary curve is again $y=x$. The question concerns the Euler equation; existence of an admissible extremal also depends on whatever endpoint data are imposed.
questions.theory: For a functional $J[y]=\int_a^bL(x,y,y\prime)dx$, smooth extremals under variations vanishing at fixed endpoints satisfy the Euler–Lagrange equation $L_y-d(L_{y\prime})/dx=0$. This follows by differentiating the functional with respect to the variation parameter and integrating the derivative term by parts. If the integrand is linear in $y\prime$, the Euler equation may reduce to an algebraic relation rather than a second-order differential equation. Boundary terms vanish for fixed-endpoint variations but generate natural boundary conditions when endpoint values are free. Satisfying the Euler equation is a necessary stationarity condition, not by itself a universal sufficient condition for a minimum. Rewriting an integrand by adding or subtracting a total derivative changes boundary terms but preserves the interior Euler equation under fixed-endpoint variations.

questions.prompt: For continuous $f$ on $[0,1]$, consider $f^2(t)=1+2\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ for every $t\in[0,1]$. Which statement is true?

options.D: There are more than two solutions

hints: At zero, $f(0)=1$ or $-1$.
On every interval where $f\ne0$, differentiating the equation gives $f\prime=1$.
questions.solution: At $t=0$, $f(0)=\pm1$. On any interval where $f$ is nonzero, its square is continuously differentiable, so $f$ is differentiable and $2ff\prime=2f$ implies $f\prime=1$. The branch starting at 1 must be $f(t)=1+t$ until a first zero, but this expression has no zero on $[0,1]$, so it holds throughout. The branch starting at $-1$ must be $f(t)=t-1$ before its first zero, which can only be at $t=1$; continuity fixes its endpoint value as zero. Both expressions satisfy the integral identity directly: their squared values are $(1+t)^2$ and $(t-1)^2$. There is no interior zero at which a new branch could be attached. Exactly two solutions exist, C.
questions.theory: Nonlinear Volterra integral equations couple the current value to the integral over all previous times. A continuous integrand makes the integral continuously differentiable by the fundamental theorem of calculus. If the left-hand side is $f^2$, differentiability of $f$ follows locally only where $f\ne0$, since there one can take a smooth signed square root. Dividing the differentiated equation by f is therefore legitimate on nonzero intervals but may discard behavior at zeros. Initial values obtained by evaluating the integral equation at its lower endpoint select possible branches. First-zero arguments then determine whether and where branching can happen. On a longer interval, solutions may remain zero for a period after reaching zero and then restart, so the specified interval matters. Finally substitute every proposed branch into the original equation, not only its differentiated form.

similar_questions.prompt: Find continuous solutions of $f^2(t)=4+2\int_0^t f(s)ds$ on $[0,1]$.

similar_questions.prompt: Give three solutions of $f^2(t)=1+2\int_0^t f(s)ds$ on $[0,2]$.

questions.prompt: A body moves freely in a uniform gravitational field. Its trajectory lies on which curve in phase space?
hints: Phase space uses position and momentum, not two position coordinates.
Eliminate time between $\dot p=-mg$ and $\dot q=p/m$, or use energy conservation.
questions.solution: Along the gravitational coordinate q, the Hamiltonian is $H=p^2/(2m)+mgq=E$. Hence $q=E/(mg)-p^2/(2m^2g)$, a parabola in the $(q,p)$ phase plane, giving B. The same follows from $p=p_0-mgt$ and $q=q_0+p_0t/m-gt^2/2$. A would apply to a force-free particle, whereas an ellipse describes a harmonic oscillator phase portrait and a hyperbola occurs for an inverted quadratic potential. For free motion with additional horizontal coordinates, those coordinates and momenta supplement this gravitational phase relation.
questions.theory: Phase space records positions and their conjugate momenta, so a phase trajectory differs from the ordinary spatial path. For one degree of freedom with mass m and potential V(q), the Hamiltonian is $p^2/(2m)+V(q)$. When it has no explicit time dependence, energy is conserved and trajectories lie on its level sets. A uniform nonzero gravitational field has a linear potential, yielding a parabolic relation between q and p. A quadratic stable potential instead produces ellipses, while a negative quadratic potential produces hyperbolas. Momentum and velocity differ only by the positive constant mass in this elementary setting, so using velocity gives the same curve type after rescaling an axis. Coordinate orientation changes the direction of the parabola but not its type. Always identify the plotted variables before applying a familiar spatial-trajectory formula.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the phase curve for a harmonic oscillator with energy E.
similar_questions.solution: For $V(q)=kq^2/2$, conservation gives $p^2/(2m)+kq^2/2=E$. For $E>0$, divide by E to obtain an ellipse with semiaxes $\sqrt{2mE}$ in momentum and $\sqrt{2E/k}$ in position.

similar_questions.prompt: What is the phase curve of a force-free particle with nonzero momentum?
similar_questions.solution: $\dot p=0$ gives $p=p_0$, while $q=q_0+p_0t/m$. Thus the phase trajectory is the horizontal line $p=p_0$ in the position–momentum plane.

questions.prompt: $X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$. Given $X$, $Y\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,X)$; given $X,Y$, $Z\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(Y,1)$. Find $E(Z)$.

No independence between X and Y is assumed: the conditional intervals explicitly depend on earlier values, and the tower property handles that dependence.
questions.theory: The law of iterated expectation, or tower property, states $E[E(U\mid\mathcal G)]=E(U)$ for integrable U and a sub-sigma-field $\mathcal G$. It permits averaging conditional distributions without first deriving the complete joint density. A uniform variable on an interval $(a,b)$ has conditional mean $(a+b)/2$ and conditional variance $(b-a)^2/12$. When the endpoints are themselves random, these expressions become random conditional moments and must then be averaged. Conditioning on both X and Y is stronger than conditioning on Y alone; another use of the tower property may simplify the expression if it depends only on Y. All variables here are bounded, so integrability is automatic. A common error is to replace every conditional uniform distribution by Uniform(0,1), thereby losing the dependence generated by random endpoints.

The two numbers involving division by 6 or 48 confuse the joint or marginal probability with the posterior; A is just the prior mass $P(N=3)$. Independence among the different $X_k$ is unnecessary for this calculation.
questions.theory: Poisson thinning states that if a Poisson count with mean $\lambda$ is independently classified into successes with probability p and failures with probability $1-p$, then the success and failure counts are independent Poisson variables with means $\lambda p$ and $\lambda(1-p)$. The marginal result also follows solely from a binomial conditional distribution given the total count. Bayes formula computes posterior probabilities by dividing a joint mass by the conditioning event mass. In this setting, after observing y successes, the total is y plus an independent Poisson failure count, so $P(N=y\mid Y=y)=e^{-\lambda(1-p)}$. This is generally different from the prior mass at y. When a randomly indexed variable is used, independence of each indexed variable from the index ensures its conditional distribution is unchanged; mutual independence of the sequence is a separate assumption.

similar_questions.solution: Given two successes, the total is $2+F$ where $F\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(3)$. Its conditional expectation is therefore $2+3=5$.

questions.prompt: Let $(N_t^1)$ and $(N_t^2)$ be independent Poisson processes of rates $a>b$. The source defines $M_t=\max\{N_t^1,N_t^2\}$ and again $M_t=\max\{N_t^1-N_t^2,0\}$. Which statement is true?

options.B: $X$ is a birth-and-death process with birth rate a and death rate b
options.D: $M$ is a pure birth process with birth rate $a+b$

hints: First distinguish the maximum of the two counts from the clipped difference.
Clipping an unconstrained difference does not create the reflected birth-and-death chain: it hides its negative depth.
questions.solution: The literal source defines M twice and never defines X, so A and B are undefined. Even if the second M is conditionally renamed $X_t=\max\{N_t^1-N_t^2,0\}$, no listed assertion is correct. A fails because X can decrease, for example when the difference goes from 1 to 0. B fails because clipping loses negative depth: from hidden difference 0 an a-jump raises X, but from hidden difference $-1$ an a-jump leaves X at zero. More concretely, the first holding time of X at zero has survival expansion $1-at+\frac12a(a+b)t^2+O(t^3)$, rather than $e^{-at}=1-at+\frac12a^2t^2+O(t^3)$ required by birth rate a. For $M=\max(N^1,N^2)$, the first jump has rate $a+b$, disproving C since $\max(a,b)=a$. D fails because while one count leads, only jumps of the leading count increase M, so its rate is a or b, not their sum. Conditional repair to $X=N^1-N^2$ without clipping would make B true as a birth-and-death chain on $\mathbb Z$; replacing M by $N^1+N^2$ would give a Poisson process of rate $a+b$. Neither repair is silently adopted.
questions.theory: Independent Poisson processes have stationary independent increments and almost surely no simultaneous jumps. Their sum is Poisson with the sum of the rates. Their difference is a continuous-time nearest-neighbor Markov chain on the integers, with upward rate a and downward rate b, often called a bilateral birth-and-death process. Applying a many-to-one transformation to a Markov chain need not preserve the Markov property. In particular, clipping negative states at zero hides how many upward jumps are needed before positivity resumes. A reflected chain, which suppresses downward jumps at zero, is a different construction from clipping an unrestricted chain after it evolves. A count maximum is nondecreasing, but its growth depends on which component leads and on their gap; monotonicity does not make it a Poisson process or a Markov pure-birth chain with a constant rate.

similar_questions.prompt: What are the transition rates of $D_t=N_t^1-N_t^2$ for rates 2 and 1?

questions.prompt: $X_i$ are iid normal with mean 2 and variance 3. Independently, $N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(4)$. Put $Y=\sum_{i=1}^NX_i$ for $N\ge1$ and $Y=0$ for $N=0$. Find $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$.

D is correct. A counts only the variability of summands at fixed N; B counts only the variability of the conditional mean; C is neither the sum of the two contributions nor the correct variance. questions.theory: For a random sum $S=\sum_{i=1}^NX_i$, where N is independent of iid summands with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, conditioning gives $E(S\mid N)=N\mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S\mid N)=N\sigma^2$. The first variance contribution reflects randomness within a fixed number of summands; the second reflects randomness in the number itself. When N is Poisson with mean $\lambda$, its mean and variance coincide, yielding $\operatorname{Var}(S)=\lambda E(X_1^2)$. The convention of an empty sum being zero makes the same conditional formulas valid at N=0. Ignoring variability of the conditional mean is a common error when the summand mean is nonzero. The dependence structure and random-count contribution are essential even when every conditional sum has a familiar distribution.

questions.prompt: $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are iid $N(\theta,\sigma^2)$ with known $\sigma^2$. Let $\bar X=n^{-1}\sum X_i$. Which is the minimum-variance unbiased estimator of $e^{2\theta}$?
hints: Use the moment-generating function of the normal sample mean.
$E(e^{2\bar X})=e^{2\theta+2\sigma^2/n}$, then apply completeness.
questions.solution: $\bar X\sim N(\theta,\sigma^2/n)$, so $E(e^{t\bar X})=\exp(t\theta+t^2\sigma^2/(2n))$. At $t=2$ the extra factor is $e^{2\sigma^2/n}$. Thus C exactly removes it and is unbiased. The sample mean is complete sufficient for the unrestricted normal mean with known variance (a full one-parameter exponential family), so Lehmann–Scheffé makes this function of it the unique MVUE. A has mean $e^{2\theta+\sigma^2/n}$; B has mean $e^{2\theta-2\sigma^2/n}$; D generally estimates a different exponential with mean $e^{2n\theta+2n\sigma^2-2\sigma^2/n}$. Hence only C works for general n and $\theta$.
questions.theory: For a normal variable with mean m and variance v, its moment-generating function is $E(e^{tX})=\exp(tm+t^2v/2)$. Exponentiating an unbiased estimator of m does not give an unbiased estimator of its exponential; an explicit variance correction is required. In a normal location model with known positive variance and unrestricted real mean, the sample sum, equivalently the sample mean, is complete sufficient because the natural parameter space is an open interval in a full exponential family. Completeness means that a statistic-based function with zero expectation for every parameter must vanish almost surely. Lehmann–Scheffé states that an unbiased function of a complete sufficient statistic is the unique minimum-variance unbiased estimator. Finite exponential moments ensure the variance here exists. The exponent multiplier must be squared in the correction term, which explains the factor 2 for estimating $e^{2\theta}$.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the MVUE of $e^\theta$ in the same known-variance normal model.
similar_questions.solution: $E(e^{\bar X})=e^{\theta+\sigma^2/(2n)}$. Therefore $e^{\bar X-\sigma^2/(2n)}$ is unbiased and is a function of the complete sufficient mean, hence is the MVUE.

questions.prompt: $X$ has density $f_\theta(x)\propto x^{\theta-1}(1-x)^{\theta-1}$ for $0<x<1$, $\theta>0$. For testing $H_0:\theta=1$ versus $H_1:\theta>1$ with one observation, what form has a size-$\alpha$ UMP critical region?
hints: Under the null X is uniform.
For any $\theta>1$, the likelihood ratio is increasing in $x(1-x)$, which is largest at the center.
questions.solution: Against a fixed $\theta>1$, the likelihood ratio to the null is $c_\theta[x(1-x)]^{\theta-1}$. It is largest when $x$ lies nearest $1/2$, so Neyman–Pearson rejects on a centered interval. Under $\theta=1$, the density is 1, so size $\alpha$ requires interval length $\alpha$, giving $((1-\alpha)/2,(1+\alpha)/2)$, C. The ordering is the same for every $\theta>1$, establishing uniform most power. A and B reject in one tail, whereas D rejects in both tails; these are lower-likelihood-ratio regions for the stated alternative. Open versus closed endpoints has no effect for a continuous distribution.
questions.theory: The Neyman–Pearson lemma selects observations with the largest likelihood ratio for a most powerful test of a simple null against a simple alternative at a prescribed size. If every parameter in a one-sided composite alternative induces the same ordering of a statistic, a common critical region is uniformly most powerful. The symmetric beta family here has natural statistic $\log[x(1-x)]$, and increasing the parameter concentrates mass near the midpoint. Under the uniform null, critical-region probability is simply its total length. Symmetry alone does not say whether to reject centrally or in the tails; the exponent sign in the likelihood ratio determines that direction. Thresholds should be calibrated under the null, not under the alternative. Continuous densities make boundary randomization unnecessary in this example.

similar_questions.prompt: For the same beta family, test $\theta=1$ against $0<\theta<1$. What is the UMP size-$\alpha$ region?
similar_questions.solution: The exponent $\theta-1$ is negative, so the likelihood ratio is largest where $x(1-x)$ is smallest, near 0 and 1. Equal symmetric tails of total null length $\alpha$ give $(0,\alpha/2)\cup(1-\alpha/2,1)$.

similar_questions.prompt: For $X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$, test $\lambda=1$ against $\lambda>1$ using one observation at size $\alpha$.
similar_questions.solution: The ratio is $\lambda e^{-(\lambda-1)x}$, decreasing in x for every alternative. Reject for $X<c$ with $1-e^{-c}=\alpha$, so $c=-\log(1-\alpha)$.

questions.prompt: $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are iid $N(\theta,1)$ and the prior is $\theta\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$. Under squared-error loss, which is the Bayes estimator of $\theta$?
hints: Squared-error loss is minimized by the posterior mean.
Add the likelihood precision n and prior precision $1/\sigma^2$.
questions.solution: The posterior kernel is $\exp\{-\frac12[n(\theta-\bar X)^2+\theta^2/\sigma^2]\}$. Completing the square gives posterior variance $(n+1/\sigma^2)^{-1}$ and mean $n\bar X/(n+1/\sigma^2)=n\sigma^2\bar X/(1+n\sigma^2)$. This mean is the Bayes estimator, C. A has the wrong shrinkage factor and omits n; B would correspond to a limiting flat prior rather than the stated finite-variance prior; D adds an unjustified nonzero prior-location term. For zero prior variance, the degenerate limit of C is zero, consistent with known $\theta=0$.
questions.theory: Under squared-error loss, conditional posterior risk decomposes as $E[(d-\theta)^2\mid X]=(d-E[\theta\mid X])^2+\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid X)$, so the posterior mean is optimal. A normal likelihood and normal prior are conjugate. Their precisions, defined as reciprocals of variances, add; the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of the sample mean and prior mean. With observation variance one, the sample mean variance is $1/n$, giving likelihood precision n. A finite zero-centered prior shrinks the data estimate toward zero, with shrinkage diminishing as n increases. Posterior variance is smaller than each of the input variances. Distinguish prior variance from observation variance: confusing them reverses the weights and can produce an estimator that fails the large-sample or concentrated-prior limits.

similar_questions.prompt: One observation $X\sim N(\theta,1)$ with prior $N(2,1)$: find the posterior mean.
similar_questions.solution: The likelihood and prior precisions are both 1, so their mean is $(X+2)/2$ and posterior variance is $1/2$. Under squared-error loss this mean is the Bayes estimator.

similar_questions.prompt: For n observations with variance 4 and prior $N(0,1)$, find the Bayes estimator.
similar_questions.solution: The likelihood precision is $n/4$ and prior precision is 1. The posterior mean is $(n/4)\bar X/(1+n/4)=n\bar X/(n+4)$; posterior variance is $4/(n+4)$.

questions.prompt: $X$ is a $p\times p$ Wishart random matrix with variance matrix $\Sigma$ and m degrees of freedom. $A_{ij}$ denotes an entry of A. Which statement is necessarily true?

options.A: $cX_{12}$ is chi-square with $m-p+1$ degrees of freedom for some suitable c
options.B: $cX_{11}$ is chi-square with $m-p+1$ degrees of freedom for some suitable c
options.C: $Y=AX$ is Wishart with variance matrix $A\Sigma A^T$ and m degrees of freedom for every nonsingular A
options.D: A $k\times k$ submatrix of X is also Wishart for $k<p$

hints: Use $X=\sum_{r=1}^mZ_rZ_r^T$ for normal vectors $Z_r$.
Wishart transformations require congruence $AXA^T$, and square submatrices must be principal.
questions.solution: Literally D does not specify a principal submatrix, and arbitrary square submatrices need not be symmetric or Wishart. For example with $p=2,k=1,\Sigma=I$, the submatrix consisting of entry $X_{12}$ can be negative, unlike a one-dimensional Wishart variable. A fails for this same signed off-diagonal entry. B is false in general: $X_{11}/\Sigma_{11}\sim\chi_m^2$, and scaling cannot change its gamma shape to $(m-p+1)/2$ when $p>1$. C fails since AX need not even be symmetric; the valid transformation is $AXA^T$. If D is intended to mean a principal submatrix $X_{II}$ using the same row and column indices, then $X_{II}=\sum Z_{r,I}Z_{r,I}^T\sim W_k(\Sigma_{II},m)$ and D is the intended answer. The literal generic submatrix claim does not support a unique true choice, so no unconditional label is assigned.
questions.theory: A Wishart matrix with integer degrees of freedom m can be represented as the sum of m outer products of independent centered normal vectors with common covariance $\Sigma$. This gives a symmetric positive semidefinite random matrix. Its diagonal entries, after division by their respective variance entries, have chi-square distributions with m degrees of freedom. Off-diagonal entries are sums of products and can have either sign; they are not generally gamma or chi-square variables. Linear transformation of the underlying normal vectors induces a congruence transformation $AXA^T$, not left multiplication alone. Selecting the same subset of coordinates in every vector gives a principal submatrix that remains Wishart. Selecting unrelated row and column sets instead produces a general cross-product matrix, without symmetry or nonnegativity. The distinction between a principal submatrix and an arbitrary submatrix is therefore mathematically essential.

similar_questions.prompt: If $X\sim W_3(I,8)$, what is the distribution of $X_{11}$?
similar_questions.solution: It is the sum of squares of eight independent standard normal first coordinates, so $X_{11}\sim\chi_8^2$, not $\chi_6^2$.

similar_questions.prompt: If $X\sim W_3(\Sigma,m)$, give the distribution of its top-left $2\times2$ block.
similar_questions.solution: Select the first two coordinates of each normal vector in the outer-product representation. They are iid $N_2(0,\Sigma_{\{1,2\},\{1,2\}})$, so the block is $W_2(\Sigma_{\{1,2\},\{1,2\}},m)$.

questions.source_note: Option C prints $AX$, not $AXA^T$. Option D prints only “$k\times k$ sub-matrix” without “principal”; arbitrary square submatrices do not remain Wishart. D is conditionally correct under the principal-submatrix interpretation, which is fully derived.

questions.prompt: In $y_i=\alpha+\beta x_i+\epsilon_i$ for $i=1,\ldots,50$, not all $x_i$ are equal. Which is an admissible leverage for observation 11?
hints: Use the diagonal of the least-squares hat matrix with an intercept.
$h_{ii}=1/50+(x_i-\bar x)^2/\sum_j(x_j-\bar x)^2$ and $h_{ii}\le1$.
questions.solution: The leverage formula gives $h_{11}\ge1/50=0.02$, excluding A and B. The hat matrix is an orthogonal projection, so its diagonal entries are at most 1, excluding D. The value 0.1 is attainable: take centered predictors $x_{11}=2$, one other value $-2$, two further values $\sqrt{21},-\sqrt{21}$, and all remaining values zero. Then the mean is zero and $\sum x_i^2=50$, yielding $h_{11}=0.02+4/50=0.1$. Thus C is admissible, and the rank assumption holds because these predictors are not all equal.
questions.theory: In ordinary least squares, the fitted response is $\hat y=Hy$ with hat matrix $H=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T$ when the design matrix has full column rank. H is a symmetric idempotent matrix, hence an orthogonal projection; its diagonal entries, called leverages, lie between zero and one and sum to the model rank. In simple regression with an intercept, centering the predictor gives $h_{ii}=1/n+(x_i-\bar x)^2/S_{xx}$, where $S_{xx}>0$ when not all predictors are equal. Consequently the intercept imposes the sharper lower bound $1/n$. Large leverage measures an unusual predictor position, not necessarily an unusually large residual or an influential observation. To establish admissibility rigorously, check both the general bounds and, when needed, construct predictor values that attain the requested leverage.

similar_questions.prompt: For n=10 simple regression, what is the leverage of an observation with $x_i=\bar x$?
similar_questions.solution: The squared deviation term is zero, so $h_{ii}=1/10=0.1$. This is the smallest possible leverage in the intercept model.

similar_questions.prompt: If n=20 and $S_{xx}=40$, find leverage when $x_i-\bar x=2$.
similar_questions.solution: $h_{ii}=1/20+4/40=0.05+0.1=0.15$. The intercept and predictor-deviation contributions must both be included.

questions.prompt: Independent identically distributed $(X_i,Y_i)$ are uniform on the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(\theta,0)$ and $(\theta,0)$ as printed, where $\theta>0$. Which statistic is sufficient for $\theta$?
hints: Check whether the printed vertices determine a nondegenerate triangle.
If the repeated vertex were $(0,\theta)$, the support constraint would be $X_i+Y_i\le\theta$.
questions.solution: The last two printed vertices are identical, so their convex hull is a line segment, not a positive-area triangle. A uniform planar density on that purported triangle cannot be normalized. Hence the stated two-dimensional uniform model is undefined and no literal sufficiency answer follows. If one conditionally corrects the repeated last vertex to $(0,\theta)$, the triangle has density $2/\theta^2$ on $x,y\ge0$, $x+y\le\theta$. The likelihood then factors as $(2/\theta^2)^n\mathbf1\{\theta\ge\max_i(X_i+Y_i)\}\prod_i\mathbf1\{X_i,Y_i\ge0\}$, proving B is sufficient under that correction. A and D can confound which coordinate maxima came from the same observation, while C does not capture the required sums. Alternatively, choosing a one-dimensional uniform law on the literal segment would be a different model, with all Y values zero and several listed statistics coinciding; that is not silently substituted for the planar triangle.
questions.theory: A statistic is sufficient when the conditional distribution of the sample given that statistic is free of the unknown parameter. The factorization theorem provides an equivalent likelihood criterion for dominated models: all parameter dependence must appear through the statistic and a parameter-dependent factor. For uniform distributions whose support depends on a scale parameter, the indicator of membership is essential and often produces an extreme-order statistic. On the right triangle $x,y\ge0$, $x+y\le\theta$, the largest observed coordinate sum determines whether every observation belongs to the support. Density normalization uses the area $\theta^2/2$. Degenerate vertex sets have zero planar area and require a different dominating measure and explicit model specification. Before applying the theorem, verify that the purported probability distribution itself exists and that the support geometry has been transcribed correctly.

similar_questions.prompt: For iid Uniform$(0,\theta)$ observations, find a sufficient statistic.
similar_questions.solution: The likelihood is $\theta^{-n}\mathbf1\{\theta\ge X_{(n)}\}\prod_i\mathbf1\{X_i\ge0\}$. Factorization shows the sample maximum $X_{(n)}$ is sufficient.

similar_questions.prompt: For iid uniform points on $[0,\theta]^2$, find a sufficient statistic.
similar_questions.solution: The joint likelihood is $\theta^{-2n}\mathbf1\{\theta\ge\max_i\max(X_i,Y_i)\}\prod_i\mathbf1\{X_i,Y_i\ge0\}$. Thus the overall coordinate maximum, rather than maximum coordinate sum, is sufficient.

questions.prompt: From N households, take samples of size $0<n<N$ to estimate the proportion with more than one earning member. Sample I uses SRS without replacement and sample II uses SRS with replacement. Let $p_i$ be sample proportions and $\sigma_i^2=\operatorname{Var}(p_i)$. Which statement is true?
hints: Both sampling schemes have unbiased sample proportions.
Derive the finite-population correction and check when its inequality is strict.
questions.solution: Write the population proportion as P. Both sample proportions have expectation P, so A and B are false. With replacement, $\sigma_2^2=P(1-P)/n$. Without replacement, the hypergeometric variance gives $\sigma_1^2=[P(1-P)/n](N-n)/(N-1)$. Thus $\sigma_1^2\le\sigma_2^2$ always, and D is false. C is strict only if $n>1$ and $0<P<1$. The stated $0<n<N$ permits $n=1$, in which case the variances are identical. It also permits populations with P=0 or P=1, giving zero variances for either scheme. Consequently no listed statement is necessarily true under the literal hypotheses. Under the additional nondegeneracy assumptions $1<n<N$ and $0<P<1$, C is the intended answer.
questions.theory: Simple random sampling without replacement selects a uniformly random subset of fixed size; with replacement it selects independent uniform population members. The sample proportion of a binary characteristic is unbiased under both designs because each draw or inclusion has the same marginal population proportion. Without replacement, negatively correlated draws reduce variance by the finite-population correction $(N-n)/(N-1)$ when the variance is expressed using $P(1-P)$. This correction equals one at n=1, is less than one at n>1, and becomes zero at a full census. If every population unit has the same binary value, both variances are zero independently of sample size. Distinguish non-strict variance reduction from strict reduction, and inspect endpoint sample sizes and degenerate populations before endorsing a universal strict inequality.

similar_questions.prompt: N=100, n=10, P=1/2: compare the two variances.
similar_questions.solution: With replacement the variance is $0.25/10=0.025$. Without replacement multiply by $90/99$, giving $1/44\approx0.022727$. This is strictly smaller because n>1 and the population is mixed.

similar_questions.prompt: N=10, n=1, P=0.3: compare variances.
similar_questions.solution: Each design draws one uniform household, so each sample proportion is Bernoulli$(0.3)$. Both variances are $0.3\cdot0.7=0.21$; there is no strict reduction.

questions.prompt: Maximize $4x+5y$ subject to $2x+3y\le14$, $x+2y\le9$, $x+y\le6$, $x,y\ge0$. What is the optimal objective value?
hints: A nonnegative combination of two constraints can bound the objective directly.
questions.solution: For every feasible point, $4x+5y=(2x+3y)+2(x+y)\le14+2\cdot6=26$. Equality requires $2x+3y=14$ and $x+y=6$, giving $(x,y)=(4,2)$. It is feasible because $x+2y=8\le9$ and both coordinates are nonnegative. Thus the upper bound is achieved and the optimum is 26, B. A and D are attainable lower values but not maxima; C exceeds the proven global bound. This gives both a feasible solution and an optimality certificate without enumerating every vertex.
questions.theory: A linear program optimizes a linear function on an intersection of half-spaces. In a bounded nonempty feasible polytope, a linear objective attains its optimum at an extreme point, though an entire edge may be optimal when the objective is parallel to it. Another method proves a global bound by taking a nonnegative linear combination of inequality constraints whose left-hand side equals the objective. Any feasible point then satisfies that bound. If a feasible point attains it, optimality is established immediately; these coefficients are dual multipliers. Constraints assigned positive multipliers must be active at an attaining point, reflecting complementary slackness. A solution of selected boundary equations must still be tested against all remaining constraints and nonnegativity. A bound alone or a feasible point alone is not a complete optimality proof.

similar_questions.prompt: Maximize $x+y$ with $x+2y\le4$, $2x+y\le4$, $x,y\ge0$.
similar_questions.solution: Adding the two constraints gives $3(x+y)\le8$. Their intersection is $x=y=4/3$, feasible and attaining $8/3$. Thus the optimum is $8/3$.

similar_questions.prompt: Maximize $3x+2y$ with $x+y\le5$, $x\le3$, $x,y\ge0$.
similar_questions.solution: Write the objective as $2(x+y)+x\le10+3=13$. The feasible point $(3,2)$ attains 13, so it is optimal.

questions.prompt: Let $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. Which functions from $\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$ to $\mathbb N$ are injective?
hints: Prime-factor uniqueness directly applies to one formula.
For the others exhibit two distinct input pairs with the same output.
questions.solution: A is injective: equality $2^m3^n=2^{m\prime}3^{n\prime}$ forces equality of the exponents of the distinct primes 2 and 3. B is not injective because it is symmetric: $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$ both give 5. C is not injective: $(3,2)$ and $(4,1)$ both give $17$, since $3^2+2^3=9+8=17=16+1=4^2+1^3$. D is not injective because $(8,1)$ and $(1,4)$ both give 64.
questions.theory: An injective function maps different domain elements to different values; to prove it, start from equality of outputs and deduce equality of every input coordinate. To disprove it, a single collision suffices, but both input pairs must actually belong to the specified domain. Unique prime factorization encodes multiple positive integer coordinates as exponents of distinct fixed primes, and comparison of prime valuations recovers those coordinates. Symmetric formulas on ordered pairs frequently fail injectivity by interchanging unequal inputs. Sums of powers can also collide even when no symmetry is present, so arithmetic examples must be verified. Products of variable powers lose information because prime valuations from the two coordinates can compensate for each other. Avoid trial examples involving irrational roots in a natural-number domain, and independently evaluate both outputs of any purported collision.

similar_questions.prompt: Is $(m,n)\mapsto5^m7^n$ injective on positive integer pairs?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. Equality of outputs forces equal 5-adic valuations and equal 7-adic valuations, recovering m and n uniquely.

similar_questions.prompt: Is $(m,n)\mapsto mn$ injective on positive integer pairs?
similar_questions.solution: No. The distinct pairs $(1,6)$ and $(2,3)$ both map to 6, so the function fails injectivity.

questions.prompt: Let $(x_n)$ be a sequence of positive real numbers. Which statements are true?

options.D: If $(x_n)$ is unbounded, then every subsequence is unbounded

hints: The two parity subsequences need to share a limit for the full sequence to converge.
For B use absolute values; for C bound successive ratios by a finite constant eventually.
questions.solution: A is false: $x_{2n}=1$, $x_{2n+1}=2$ gives two different limits. B is true because $x_n=|(-1)^nx_n|$, and absolute value preserves limits. Positivity also forces a signed limit to be zero by comparing the signs on the parity subsequences. C is true under the ordinary meaning of existence of a finite real limit: eventually $x_{n+1}/x_n\le M$ for some $M>0$, hence $x_n\le x_NM^{n-N}$ and $x_n^{1/n}$ is bounded, with finitely many early terms harmless. D is false: $x_{2n}=n$, $x_{2n+1}=1$ is unbounded but has a bounded odd subsequence. Thus B and C are correct. If an infinite extended ratio limit were allowed, C would require qualification; for example $x_n=n!$ has unbounded roots.
questions.theory: A sequence converges when all sufficiently late terms are uniformly near one limit. Convergence of separately indexed subsequences implies convergence of the full sequence only when their limits agree and together they cover its tail. Continuous functions, such as absolute value, preserve convergence. Positive sequences are particularly amenable to multiplicative bounds: an eventual finite upper bound M on successive ratios gives at most geometric growth, and taking nth roots then yields a bounded sequence. This is related to the ratio and root tests, but no series convergence claim is needed here. Unboundedness means that some arbitrarily large terms exist, not that every late term is large or that every subsequence is unbounded. When a limit is said to exist without mention of extended real values, the standard interpretation is a finite limit; distinguish that from divergence to infinity.

similar_questions.prompt: If even terms tend to 3 and odd terms tend to 3, does the whole sequence converge?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. For any tolerance, choose bounds for each parity subsequence and then take an index beyond both. Every later term belongs to one parity and lies within the tolerance of 3.

similar_questions.prompt: Show that $x_{n+1}\le2x_n$ for positive $x_n$ makes nth roots bounded.

questions.prompt: Let $f(x)=e^x$ on $\mathbb R$. Which statements are correct?

options.A: There exists $C>0$ with $|f(x)-1-x|\le Cx^2$ for every real x
options.C: There exists $C>0$ with $|f(x)-1-x-x^2/2-x^3/3!|\le Cx^4$ for every real x

hints: Taylor remainder bounds use a supremum of the next derivative on the relevant interval.
On $[-1,1]$, every derivative of the exponential is at most e; globally exponential growth defeats any polynomial bound.
questions.solution: Taylor theorem at zero gives the second-order remainder $e^\xi x^3/3!$ with $\xi$ between zero and x. On $[-1,1]$ its absolute value is at most $(e/6)|x|^3$, proving B. The third-order remainder is $e^\eta x^4/4!$, bounded by $(e/24)x^4$ on that interval, proving D. A and C fail as $x\to+\infty$: the exponential minus any fixed polynomial, divided by the proposed polynomial power, tends to infinity. Thus no fixed global C works, and the correct options are B and D. At x=0 all remainder inequalities hold with both sides zero.
questions.theory: Taylor theorem with Lagrange remainder expresses a smooth function near a base point as its Taylor polynomial of degree m plus $f^{(m+1)}(\xi)x^{m+1}/(m+1)!$ for an intermediate point. A uniform bound on the next derivative over a compact interval gives one constant valid for every point in that interval. This is an estimate of the remainder, not an assertion that the remainder is exactly one fixed multiple of that power. For the exponential, all derivatives equal the exponential itself, which is bounded on compact intervals and unbounded on the whole real line. Local big-O estimates therefore do not automatically extend globally. As x tends to positive infinity, exponential growth dominates any finite polynomial. Include absolute values for odd remainder powers and check the base point separately if dividing by a power of x.

similar_questions.prompt: Bound $|e^x-1|$ on $[-2,2]$ by a multiple of $|x|$.
similar_questions.solution: Mean value theorem gives $e^x-1=e^\xi x$ with $|\xi|\le2$. Hence $|e^x-1|\le e^2|x|$ throughout the interval.

similar_questions.prompt: Prove $|\sin x-x|\le|x|^3/6$ for all real x.
similar_questions.solution: Taylor theorem at zero through degree 2 uses the third derivative $-\cos\xi$, whose absolute value is at most 1 globally. The remainder is $-\cos\xi\,x^3/6$, yielding the global bound.

questions.prompt: Which functions are uniformly continuous on $(0,1)$?
hints: A continuous extension to the closed interval gives uniform continuity.
C tends to zero at the left endpoint and D tends to one; A and B have bad paired sequences near zero.
questions.solution: C extends continuously to [0,1] by value 0 at zero, because $|x\sin(1/x)|\le x$. D extends continuously by value 1, using $\sin x/x\to1$. The extensions are uniformly continuous by Heine–Cantor, hence so are their restrictions. A fails with $x_n=1/(n+1)$ and $y_n=1/(n+2)$: their distances vanish while reciprocal values differ by 1. B fails with $x_n=1/(2\pi n+\pi/2)$ and $y_n=1/(2\pi n+3\pi/2)$: distances vanish while sine values are 1 and $-1$. Thus C and D alone are uniformly continuous.
questions.theory: Uniform continuity requires one input-distance bound to work simultaneously at every point of the domain. On a compact interval, continuity implies uniform continuity by the Heine–Cantor theorem. A continuous function on an open bounded interval that extends continuously to its endpoints therefore inherits uniform continuity. Conversely, a uniformly continuous real-valued function carries Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences, and thus has finite endpoint limits on a bounded interval. To disprove uniform continuity directly, construct two sequences whose distances tend to zero but whose function-value distances stay bounded away from zero. Oscillation can destroy uniform continuity near an excluded endpoint, but an amplitude tending to zero can suppress that oscillation sufficiently for a continuous extension. An unbounded derivative is not itself a proof of failure; $x\sin(1/x)$ illustrates this pitfall.

similar_questions.prompt: Is $\sqrt x$ uniformly continuous on $(0,1)$?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. It extends continuously to [0,1]. Also $|\sqrt x-\sqrt y|\le\sqrt{|x-y|}$, so choosing input tolerance $\varepsilon^2$ gives an explicit uniform bound.

similar_questions.prompt: Is $\log x$ uniformly continuous on $(0,1)$?
similar_questions.solution: No. Take $x_n=e^{-n}$ and $y_n=e^{-(n+1)}$. Their distance tends to zero while their logarithms differ by 1, violating uniform continuity.

questions.prompt: Let $0<y\le x$ and let n be a positive integer. Which inequalities hold in general?
hints: Integrate $nt^{n-1}$ from y to x.
The derivative is bounded between $ny^{n-1}$ and $nx^{n-1}$ on that interval.
questions.solution: $x^n-y^n=\int_y^xnt^{n-1}dt$. Because $t^{n-1}$ is nondecreasing for positive t and integer $n\ge1$, this integral lies between $ny^{n-1}(x-y)$ and $nx^{n-1}(x-y)$. Thus A and D hold. B and C fail, for example at $n=2,x=2,y=1$: the difference is 3, the y-based bound is 2 and the x-based bound is 4. Equality holds in all expressions when x=y, and for n=1, but these special cases do not make B or C generally valid.
questions.theory: If a differentiable function has derivative bounded between m and M on an interval, the mean value theorem bounds its increment between $m(x-y)$ and $M(x-y)$ for x at least y. The same result follows by integrating the derivative when the fundamental theorem applies. For the power function $t^n$ on positive arguments, the derivative $nt^{n-1}$ is nondecreasing, giving endpoint derivative bounds. similar_questions.prompt: For $f(x)=x$ on $[0,2]$ with n equal intervals, compute the upper-minus-lower sum.

similar_questions.prompt: Evaluate $\sum_{n=1}^\infty1/[(n+1)(n+2)]$.

If $n\ge2$, this derivative is absolutely integrable near zero, and the continuous extension is of bounded variation. The subtracted $x^k$ also has finite variation; for k=0 the prescribed zero value at zero introduces only a finite jump. For n=1, choose extrema $x_j=1/(2j+1)$, where $\sin(c/x_j)=(-1)^j$. Variation along consecutive extrema is at least $\sum_j(x_j+x_{j+1})$, which diverges harmonically. For n=0 the same extrema have values $\pm1$, giving infinite variation. A and C include n=1, and B includes n=0, so each is false; D is true.
questions.theory: The total variation of f on an interval is the supremum, over all finite partitions, of the sum of absolute increments. A function has bounded variation if this supremum is finite. Sums and differences of bounded-variation functions remain of bounded variation, and a finite jump contributes finite variation. For an absolutely continuous function, total variation equals the integral of the absolute derivative, which gives a convenient sufficient criterion when a derivative is integrable. Oscillatory expressions approaching an endpoint can be tested through sequences of alternating extrema; their increment sums may diverge even when the function itself tends to zero. The oscillation amplitude must decay fast enough relative to its frequency. A continuous function can have infinite variation, and subtracting a smooth power cannot cancel that defect because otherwise the original function would be a sum of two bounded-variation functions.

similar_questions.prompt: Is $x^3\sin(1/x)$, extended by zero, of bounded variation on $[0,1]$?

similar_questions.prompt: Is $\sin(1/x)$, assigned any finite value at zero, of bounded variation?
similar_questions.solution: No. Alternating extrema arbitrarily near zero take values 1 and $-1$. Each neighboring pair contributes 2, so partitions with arbitrarily many such points have arbitrarily large total variation.

They correspond to multiplication by a complex scalar after identifying the plane with the complex numbers; the orientation convention determines the sign of the imaginary coordinate. A necessary derivative constraint becomes sufficient for a possible derivative by constructing a linear map with that matrix. Do not assume that every function with this discrete symmetry is holomorphic; the symmetry constrains its derivative at the fixed point but does not impose the Cauchy–Riemann equations at every other point.

similar_questions.prompt: Find all real $2\times2$ matrices commuting with $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$.

similar_questions.prompt: Does $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\-4&3\end{pmatrix}$ commute with a quarter-turn?

B has determinant r, hence determinant 1 at $(1,\pi)$ and is locally invertible despite global angular periodicity. C has $f\prime(0)=1$, but for nonzero x its derivative is $1+4x\sin(1/x)-2\cos(1/x)$. At $x=1/(2\pi n)$ it equals $-1$; at $x=1/((2n+1)\pi)$ it equals 3. Smoothness near the point, not just differentiability at the point, is part of the hypothesis. Global injectivity is unnecessary; polar coordinates near a positive-radius point give a standard local example despite angle periodicity. For a continuous real-valued function on an interval, injectivity is equivalent to strict monotonicity. A derivative taking both positive and negative values in every interval around a point therefore obstructs local injectivity. A zero derivative alone does not prove failure of inversion, since $x^3$ is invertible; explicit repeated values or loss of monotonicity are stronger arguments. Always verify the exact theorem hypotheses before using a nonzero derivative as a certificate.

similar_questions.prompt: Does $f(x)=x^3$ have a local inverse at zero?
similar_questions.solution: Yes: it is strictly increasing everywhere and its inverse is the real cube root. Its derivative is zero at zero, so the smooth inverse theorem does not apply and the inverse is not differentiable there.

similar_questions.prompt: Is $(r,\theta)\mapsto(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ locally invertible at r=0?
similar_questions.solution: No. All points $(0,\theta)$ map to $(0,0)$, including distinct nearby angles. The Jacobian determinant r vanishes, and this explicit collision establishes failure of local injectivity.

questions.prompt: Let $C_0(\mathbb R)$ be continuous functions with $f(x)\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$, equipped with the uniform norm. For $f_n,f\in C_0(\mathbb R)$, which statements are correct?

options.A: Uniform convergence on compact sets implies $\|f_n-f\|\to0$
options.B: $\|f_n-f\|\to0$ implies uniform convergence on compact sets
options.C: Uniform convergence on compact sets is equivalent to $\|f_n-f\|\to0$

hints: The supremum on a compact subset is bounded by the supremum over the whole line.
Consider a fixed-height compactly supported bump translated toward infinity.
questions.solution: For any compact K, $\sup_{x\in K}|f_n(x)-f(x)|\le\|f_n-f\|_\infty$, so B is true. Conversely let $\phi(x)=\max(1-|x|,0)$ and $f_n(x)=\phi(x-n)$, with $f=0$. Each is in $C_0(\mathbb R)$; on every fixed compact set, $f_n$ is eventually identically zero. Yet $\|f_n\|_\infty=1$ for every n. Thus A and C fail; D fails because the implication in B always holds. Only B is correct.
questions.theory: The uniform norm measures the supremum over the entire domain, and its convergence controls every subset simultaneously. Compact-uniform convergence measures the supremum on each fixed compact subset, allowing the relevant index to depend on that subset. On a noncompact domain, mass or peaks can escape to infinity, making compact convergence strictly weaker than global uniform convergence. Membership of each function in $C_0$ means that each individual function vanishes at infinity, but does not give a uniform tail bound over an entire sequence. A translated compactly supported bump is therefore a useful counterexample. If a sequence additionally has uniformly small tails, compact-uniform convergence can imply norm convergence by splitting the domain into one large compact set and its complement. The distinction lies in the order and uniformity of the quantifiers.

similar_questions.prompt: For $f_n(x)=e^{-x^2}/n$, compare the two convergence notions.
similar_questions.solution: The supremum is $1/n$, so $f_n\to0$ in uniform norm. The same bound controls every compact subset, establishing compact-uniform convergence as well.

similar_questions.prompt: For $f_n(x)=e^{-(x-n)^2}$, does compact-uniform convergence imply norm convergence here?
similar_questions.solution: On a fixed compact set, the distance to n tends uniformly to infinity, so $f_n\to0$ there. Its supremum is always 1 at x=n, so there is no convergence in uniform norm.

questions.prompt: A is an $m\times n$ matrix. $A(1,:)$ deletes row 1, $A(:,1)$ deletes column 1, and $A(1,1)$ deletes both. Which statements hold?

questions.solution: A holds by deleting one row and one column successively, each reducing rank by at most one, and submatrices cannot increase rank. B is false for $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$: deleting row 1 leaves rank 1 while deleting column 1 leaves rank 0. For C, equality with the row-deleted rank means row 1 is a combination of the other rows. The same relation survives deleting column 1, so deleting row 1 from $A(:,1)$ does not reduce rank. Its rank already equals rank A by hypothesis, proving C. D follows by adding the inequalities $\operatorname{rank}A(1,:)\ge\operatorname{rank}A-1$ and $\operatorname{rank}A(:,1)\ge\operatorname{rank}A-1$. Thus A,C,D hold.
questions.theory: Matrix rank is both the dimension of the row space and the dimension of the column space. Removing one row can reduce the row-span dimension by at most one; the corresponding statement applies to removing one column. Every submatrix has rank at most that of the original matrix. Equality after row deletion means that the deleted row was dependent on the retained rows. Any coordinate restriction preserves a linear dependence, which is why that row remains redundant after deleting a column. This elementary dependency argument proves stronger statements than merely combining the numerical rank bounds. Row deletion and column deletion need not have identical effects: the structure of a particular row and column matters. When checking a universal rank identity, tiny matrices with a zero column or repeated rows often give decisive counterexamples.

similar_questions.prompt: Can deleting one row reduce rank by two?
similar_questions.solution: No. Restoring one row adds one vector to the row span and raises its dimension by at most one. Therefore the original rank exceeds the row-deleted rank by at most one.

similar_questions.prompt: For $A=I_3$, delete its first row and first column. What ranks result?
similar_questions.solution: A has rank 3. Each single deletion has rank 2. Deleting both yields $I_2$ of rank 2, showing that two deletions need not cause a total rank loss of two.

questions.prompt: Let $M\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ with $M\ne0,I_n$ and $M^2=M$. Which statements are true?

options.B: Every nonzero $X\in\operatorname{Col}(M)$ is an eigenvector for eigenvalue 1
options.C: Every $X\notin\operatorname{Null}(M)$ is an eigenvector for eigenvalue 1
