Decompose any vector as $X=MX+(X-MX)$.
questions.solution: A is true by the definition $MX=0X$. Since $M\ne I$ and is idempotent, the kernel is nonzero: otherwise M would be invertible and $M^2=M$ would imply M=I. For B, write $X=MY$; then $MX=M^2Y=MY=X$, so every nonzero image vector is a 1-eigenvector. C fails for $M=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and $X=(1,1)^T$: it is not in the kernel but $MX=(1,0)^T\ne X$. D holds because $MX$ lies in the image and $M(X-MX)=0$. The sum is in fact direct, since an image vector in the kernel is both fixed and annihilated. Thus A,B,D are correct.
questions.theory: An idempotent linear map satisfies $M^2=M$ and is a projection onto its image along its kernel. It need not be an orthogonal projection unless it is also symmetric in the real standard inner product. Idempotence forces every eigenvalue to satisfy $\lambda^2=\lambda$, hence to be 0 or 1. The polynomial $t(t-1)$ has distinct roots, so every idempotent matrix is diagonalizable. Every vector decomposes uniquely into its image component $MX$ and kernel component $(I-M)X$. Being outside the kernel only says that the image component is nonzero; it does not remove the kernel component or make the vector itself fixed. Nonzero and nonidentity assumptions ensure that both eigenspaces occur. The rank is the dimension of the 1-eigenspace and the nullity is the dimension of the 0-eigenspace.

similar_questions.prompt: For $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, find image and kernel.
similar_questions.solution: $M(x,y)=(x+y,0)$, so the image is span$(1,0)$ and kernel is span$(1,-1)$. The map is idempotent but not symmetric, giving an oblique projection.

similar_questions.prompt: Decompose $(3,4)$ for $M=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$.
similar_questions.solution: The image component is $M(3,4)=(3,0)$ and the kernel component is $(0,4)$. Their sum is the original vector, and their respective subspaces intersect only at zero.

options.D: $W_1+W_2$ is a proper subset of $M_2(\mathbb R)$

Their intersection consists of vectors satisfying both defining constraints. The dimension formula $\dim(U+V)=\dim U+\dim V-\dim(U\cap V)$ corrects for directions counted twice. Parameter descriptions must be compared using independent parameters before equating entries; do not assume that identically named parameters in two different definitions are automatically the same until membership equality forces it. A nonzero shared direction disproves a trivial-intersection claim. A dimension strictly below the ambient dimension proves that a subspace is proper. similar_questions.prompt: In $\mathbb R^3$, let U=span$(e_1,e_2)$ and V=span$(e_2,e_3)$. Find intersection and sum.

similar_questions.prompt: Can two two-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb R^4$ have a three-dimensional sum?

options.C: The eigenvalues of A are roots of 1

C is false because zero is not a root of unity. B is false for the nonzero nilpotent $A=E_{12}$, whose column space is span$(e_1)$. For an n-dimensional matrix, this gives characteristic polynomial $t^n$, and Cayley–Hamilton bounds the nilpotency index by n. A nilpotent matrix is diagonalizable only if it is zero, since a diagonalizable matrix with all eigenvalues zero is similar to the zero diagonal matrix. Nevertheless a sufficiently high power is zero and therefore diagonalizable. Adding the identity produces a unipotent matrix with eigenvalues one, but eigenvalues being roots of unity does not itself imply the matrix has finite order; nontrivial Jordan blocks prevent that conclusion in characteristic zero. Nilpotence is also distinct from a zero column space, which would force the original matrix itself to vanish.

similar_questions.prompt: If a $5\times5$ matrix is nilpotent, what power is guaranteed to vanish?

similar_questions.prompt: Can a nonzero real nilpotent matrix be symmetric?
similar_questions.solution: No. Real symmetric matrices are orthogonally diagonalizable. Nilpotence forces all diagonalized eigenvalues to zero, hence the matrix itself is zero.

questions.theory: An orthogonal real square matrix is characterized by $V^TV=I$, which says exactly that its columns form an orthonormal basis. Its transpose is its inverse, so its rows are also orthonormal and $VV^T=I$. Orthogonal transformations preserve inner products, lengths and angles, and their determinant is either 1 or $-1$, distinguishing orientation-preserving and orientation-reversing transformations. Orthogonality is a relation involving a product with the transpose; it is not the same as symmetry, which equates the matrix itself with its transpose. A rotation is typically orthogonal without being symmetric. For rectangular matrices, orthonormal columns give $V^TV=I$ but $VV^T$ is generally a projection rather than the identity, so the square-matrix hypothesis matters. A set of n orthonormal vectors in n dimensions automatically forms a basis.

similar_questions.prompt: Is a planar rotation by $\pi/3$ symmetric?

similar_questions.prompt: If a real matrix is both orthogonal and symmetric, what does its square equal?
similar_questions.solution: Orthogonality gives $V^TV=I$ and symmetry gives $V^T=V$, hence $V^2=I$. Its eigenvalues can therefore only be 1 or $-1$.

questions.prompt: For a function $f:[0,1]\to(0,1)$, which statements are FALSE?

options.A: If f is onto, then f is continuous
options.B: If f is continuous, then f is not onto
options.C: If f is one-to-one, then f is continuous
options.D: If f is continuous, then f is not one-to-one

hints: Use compactness to rule out continuous surjections onto an open interval.
An affine map into the interval can be injective; swapping two of its output values preserves injectivity but destroys continuity.
questions.solution: B is true: the continuous image of compact [0,1] is compact, whereas (0,1) is not compact, so no continuous map is onto. A is false: define $f(x)=x$ for $0<x<1$ and $f(0)=f(1)=1/2$; it is onto but discontinuous. D is false for the continuous injection $f(x)=(x+1)/3$. C is false as well: start with this affine injection and swap its values at x=1/3 and x=2/3, leaving all other values unchanged. questions.prompt: Let $X=\mathbb N\cup\{\infty,-\infty\}$. Its open subsets U satisfy either $U\subseteq\mathbb N$ or $X\setminus U$ is finite. Set $A=\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$ and $B=\mathbb N\cup\{-\infty\}$. Which sets are compact?
hints: A neighborhood of either added point covers all but finitely many natural numbers.
The intersection is the infinite discrete subspace of natural numbers.
questions.solution: A is compact: in any relative open cover, choose one member containing $\infty$. Its defining open set in X is cofinite, so it covers all but finitely many points of A; finitely many further members finish the cover. B has the same property. Option B is the singleton $\{-\infty\}$, compact in every topology. $A\cup B=X$ is compact, either as a finite union of compact subsets or directly by choosing neighborhoods of both added points and covering the finite remainder. But $A\cap B=\mathbb N$ is an infinite discrete subspace, covered by its singletons without a finite subcover. Thus A,B,C are correct and D false. The space is compact but its two added points cannot be separated by disjoint neighborhoods.
questions.theory: Compactness means that every open cover has a finite subcover, and it does not require a Hausdorff topology. In a cofinite-neighborhood construction, choosing one cover member containing a special point often leaves only a finite remainder, making compactness immediate. Every finite subset is compact in any topology, and a finite union of compact subsets is compact. Subspace topology must be used when considering a subset: natural-number singletons are open here, so the induced topology on the natural numbers is discrete and an infinite discrete set is not compact. A subset of a compact space need not be compact unless appropriate conditions such as closedness are available. In non-Hausdorff spaces, compact sets need not be closed, and intersecting compact subsets can even give a noncompact set, as this example demonstrates.

similar_questions.prompt: Is $\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$ compact when naturals are isolated and infinity has cofinite neighborhoods?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. Any open cover has a member containing infinity and hence all but finitely many naturals. One member for each remaining point produces a finite subcover.

similar_questions.prompt: Is an infinite discrete set compact?
similar_questions.solution: No. The collection of all singleton open sets covers it, and every finite subcollection covers only finitely many points, so no finite subcover exists.
